docs.title: Definitions & Forward Pass
docs.text:
General forward pass through the network structure is defined as follows.

Definition 1.1.1 : General Forward Pass

  • External inputs at time \(t\) : \(x^{\text{in}}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^m\)
  • Unit outputs at time \(t\) : \(y(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\)

  • Augmented input vector at time \(t\) : \(x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m+n}\)

    \[ x_k(t)= \begin{cases}x_k^{\text {in }}(t) & \text { if } k \in I \\ y_k(t) & \text { if } k \in U\end{cases} \]

    \(x(t)\) is a concatenation of inputs \(x^{\text{in}}(t)\) and outputs \(y(t)\), where \(U\) is the indices for \(y_k(t)\), and \(I\) is the indices for \(x^{\text{in}}(t)\). We use the convention that \(x_k(t)\) and \(y_k(t)\) correspond to the same unit when \(k\in U\).

  • Weight matrix : \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(m+n)}\), Entry \(w_{kl}\) connects \(x_l(t)\) to unit \(k\).

  • Pre-activation net input at time \(t+1\) : \(s(t+1)\in\mathbb{R}^n\)

    \[ \begin{equation*} s_{k}(t+1)=\sum_{l \in U} w_{k l} y_{l}(t)+\sum_{l \in I} w_{k l} x_{l}^{\text {in }}(t)=\sum_{l \in U \cup I} w_{k l} x_{l}(t) \end{equation*} \]

  • Updated unit outputs at time \(t+1\) : \(y(t+1)\in\mathbb{R}^n\)

    \[ \begin{equation*} y_{k}(t+1)=f_{k}\left(s_{k}(t+1)\right) \end{equation*} \]
\[ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}x^{\mathrm{in}}(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix}}_{x(t)} \xrightarrow{\ W\ }s(t+1)\xrightarrow{\ f\ }y(t+1). \]

Figure 1.1.1 : Forward pass diagram.

Note that all connections are treated as having a one-time-step delay: inputs at time \(t\) can influence outputs only at \(t+1\).

Assuming our task is a sequential supervised learning task, we define the network error as follows.

Definition 1.1.2 : Network Error

  • Error for unit \(k\) at time \(t\) : \(e_{k}(t)\)

    Let \(T(t)\) denote the set of indices \(k \in U\) for which there exists a specified target value \(d_{k}(t)\) that the output of the \(k\) th unit should match at time \(t\).

    \[ e_{k}(t)= \begin{cases}d_{k}(t)-y_{k}(t) & \text { if } k \in T(t) \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} \]

  • Negative overall network error at time \(t\) : \(J(t)\)

    \[ \begin{equation*} J(t)=-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{k \in U}\left[e_{k}(t)\right]^{2} \end{equation*} \]

Our goal is to maximize the negative total error \(J^{\text {total }}\left(t^{\prime}, t\right)\),

\[ \begin{equation*} J^{\text {total }}\left(t^{\prime}, t\right)=\sum_{\tau=t^{\prime}+1}^{t} J(\tau) \end{equation*} \]

One natural way to make the weight changes is along a constant positive multiple of the performance measure gradient, so that

\[ \begin{equation*} \Delta w_{i j}=\eta \frac{\partial J^{\operatorname{total}}\left(t^{\prime}, t\right)}{\partial w_{i j}} \end{equation*} \]

docs.title: Back Propagation Through Time
docs.text:
When we unroll the recurrent network through time, we obtain a feedforward network which has a layer for each time step. Note that each unit and connection in the original network has a copy at each corresponding time step in the unrolled network. The key value of this conceptualization is that it allows one to regard the problem of training a recurrent network as a corresponding problem of training a feedforward network with certain constraints imposed on its weights.

Figure 1.1.2 : Unrolled recurrent network across time steps.

This also means that we can perform standard back propagation algorithm for feedforward nets in recurrent networks. We introduce a general form of backpropagation through time (BPTT), \(BPTT(h; h')\). The gradient equations below assume fixed weights throughout the forward trajectory and an initial state independent of those weights. If weights change while states or sensitivities from earlier steps are retained, the resulting online update is generally an approximation to the fixed-weight gradient.

Definition 1.1.3 : General Back Propagation Through Time

\[BPTT(h; h')\]

  • Unroll length : \(h\)

    When we calculate the gradient at time \(t\), we retain the transitions producing outputs at times \(t-h+1,\dots,t\), treating \(y(t-h)\) as a fixed boundary state. At the beginning of a sequence, clamp this boundary to the initial time \(t_0\).

    This factor controls the truncation length. When \(h=\infty\), we maintain the full history of the network, and thus we compute the exact gradient. When the retained window does not reach the initial state, the gradient generally omits dependencies through the boundary state.

  • Update period : \(h'\)

    We compute the truncated gradient and update weights every \(h'\) steps, with \(1\le h'\le h\).

    The update objective is \(J^{\text{total}}(t-h',t)=\sum_{\tau=t-h'+1}^{t}J(\tau)\). Recall that the first argument of \(J^{\text{total}}\) is excluded from the sum.

Concept 1.1.4 : Base BPTT Equations

For a differentiable objective \(F\) that depends on the outputs over \((t_0,t]\), let \(g_k(\tau;F)\) be its direct derivative with respect to \(y_k(\tau)\), treating the outputs at different times as independent arguments. Let \(e_k(\tau;F)\) include both this direct contribution and the contribution through future recurrent states, and define

\[ \delta_k(\tau;F)=\frac{\partial F}{\partial s_k(\tau)}. \]

They satisfy the backward recurrences (with \(\tau\) stepping down from \(t\) to \(t_0+1\))

\[ e_k(\tau;F)= \begin{cases} g_k(t;F), & \tau=t, \\ g_k(\tau;F)+\displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in U} w_{\ell k}\delta_\ell(\tau+1;F), & t_0<\tau<t. \end{cases} \] \[ \delta_k(\tau;F)=f'_k\big(s_k(\tau)\big)e_k(\tau;F). \]

For \(F=\sum_\tau a_\tau J(\tau)\), the direct term is \(g_k(\tau;F)=a_\tau e_k(\tau)\), where \(e_k(\tau)\) is the target-minus-output error in Definition 1.1.2. Distinguishing direct and recurrent contributions avoids counting future losses twice.

The weight-gradient then collects contributions from each unrolled step:

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial w_{ij}}=\sum_{\tau=t_0}^{t-1}\delta_i(\tau+1;F)x_j(\tau) \]

Concept 1.1.5 : \(BPTT(h; h')\) Equations

At an update time \(t\) (performed once every \(h'\) steps), \(BPTT(h; h')\):

  1. Chooses the epoch objective

    \[ F = J^{\text{total}}(t-h',t)=\sum_{\tau=t-h'+1}^{t} J(\tau), \]

  2. Backpropagates only through the last \(h\) steps, i.e. it computes Concept 1.1.4 but restricts the recursion to \(\tau\in[t-h+1,t]\) and treats \(y(t-h)\) as constant. Only losses in \([t-h'+1,t]\) contribute direct error terms:

    \[ e_k(\tau;J^{\text{total}})= \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{\partial J(t)}{\partial y_k(t)}, & \tau=t \\ \displaystyle \frac{\partial J(\tau)}{\partial y_k(\tau)}+\sum_{\ell\in U} w_{\ell k}\delta_\ell(\tau+1;J^{\text{total}}), & t-h'+1\le \tau < t \\ \displaystyle \sum_{\ell\in U} w_{\ell k}\delta_\ell(\tau+1;J^{\text{total}}), & t-h+1 \le \tau < t-h'+1 \\ 0, & \tau < t-h+1 \end{cases} \] \[ \delta_k(\tau;J^{\text{total}})= \begin{cases} f'_k\big(s_k(\tau)\big)e_k(\tau;J^{\text{total}}), & t-h+1\le\tau\le t \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

  3. Uses the truncated sum:

    \[ \frac{\partial J^{\text{total}}(t-h',t)}{\partial w_{ij}} \approx\sum_{\tau=t-h}^{t-1}\delta_i\big(\tau+1;J^{\text{total}}(t-h',t)\big)x_j(\tau) \]

    (the approximation is precisely the truncation to the interval \([t-h, t]\)).

Thus, \(BPTT(h; h')\) uses an approximate gradient of \(J^{\text{total}}(t-h',t)\), backpropagating through the last \(h\) time steps and injecting only the direct errors occurring in the last \(h'\) time steps.

Figure 1.1.3 : Truncated BPTT window over the unrolled sequence.

By controlling parameters \(h\) and \(h'\), we can achieve various forms of BPTT.

Definition 1.1.6 : Real-Time BPTT

\[BPTT(\infty; 1)\]

Real-Time BPTT computes a gradient at every time step (\(h'=1\)), backpropagating through the full history (\(h=\infty\)). It is exact under the fixed-weight assumption above; its work and stored history grow with elapsed sequence length, so “real-time” does not mean constant work per step.

Figure 1.1.4 : Real-time BPTT with full-history backprop each step.

Definition 1.1.7 : Epochwise BPTT

\[BPTT(L; L),\qquad L=t_1-t_0.\]

Epochwise BPTT runs forward over an interval \([t_0,t_1]\), then performs one backward pass and one weight update. With a fixed initial state and no intermediate weight updates, this is the exact gradient over the epoch. The implementation and plot legends use \(BPTT(\infty,\infty)\) informally to mean “full history, update at the end of the finite epoch.”

Figure 1.1.5 : Epochwise BPTT backpropagating over the full sequence.

Definition 1.1.8 : Truncated Real-Time BPTT

\[BPTT(h; 1)\]

Truncated Real-Time BPTT is the same as real-time BPTT (Definition 1.1.6) but backpropagates only through the last \(h\) steps.

Definition 1.1.9 : Truncated Gradients with Epochwise Updates

Another convention truncates the backward path of each loss \(J(\tau)\) to at most \(h\) transitions, accumulates these approximate gradients over the epoch, and updates once at its end. This preserves losses throughout the epoch; backpropagating only from the final \(h\) steps would discard earlier losses. This per-loss convention differs from the single shared history window in Concept 1.1.5 and should not be identified with \(BPTT(h;\infty)\).

docs.title: Real-Time Recurrent Learning
docs.text:
Definition 1.1.10 : Real-Time Recurrent Learning

For each \(k \in U, i \in U, j \in U \cup I\), and \(t_{0} \leq t \leq t_{1}\), we define

\[ p_{i j}^{k}(t)=\frac{\partial y_{k}(t)}{\partial w_{i j}} \]

From the chain rule and differentiation of Definition 1.1.1 and Definition 1.1.2, we find that

\[ \frac{\partial J(t)}{\partial w_{i j}}=\sum_{k \in U} e_{k}(t) p_{i j}^{k}(t) \] \[ p_{i j}^{k}(t+1)=f_{k}^{\prime}\left(s_{k}(t+1)\right)\left[\sum_{l \in U} w_{k l} p_{i j}^{l}(t)+\delta_{i k} x_{j}(t)\right] \]

with the initial condition

\[ p_{i j}^{k}\left(t_{0}\right)=\frac{\partial y_{k}\left(t_{0}\right)}{\partial w_{i j}}=0. \]

The zero initial condition assumes \(y(t_0)\) does not depend on the weights. Using this recurrence, we can compute \(\frac{\partial J(t)}{\partial w_{i j}}\) online, subject to the fixed-weight qualification stated above.

Unlike back propagation through time, real time recurrent learning allows gradient computation in the same direction as the forward pass, without maintaining specific history of the network.

For a dense network with \(m=O(n)\), maintaining \(p_{i j}^{k}(t)\) requires \(\Theta(n^3)\) space and \(\Theta(n^4)\) time per step. The 1995 paper's exact hybrid algorithm, \(FP/BPTT(h)\), uses \(\Theta(n^3+nh)\) space and \(\Theta(n^3+n^4/h)\) amortized time per step. Choosing \(h=\Theta(n)\) gives \(\Theta(n^3)\) time per step, improving on RTRL's \(\Theta(n^4)\) bound. These bounds are for the dense, fully trainable network; they do not give a general \(\Theta(n^2)\) exact algorithm.

docs.title: Teacher Forcing
docs.text:
Definition 1.1.11 : Teacher Forcing

During teacher forced training, whenever a target exists for unit \(k\) at time \(t\) (i.e., \(k\in T(t)\)), the network feeds the target back in place of the unit’s own output for all subsequent computations at that time step.

\[ x_k(t)= \begin{cases} x^{\text{in}}_k(t), & k\in I,\\ d_k(t), & k\in T(t),\\ y_k(t), & k\in U\setminus T(t). \end{cases} \]

In BPTT, we cut off the error flow from future time steps into the teacher-forced node and use only the direct loss term at that step. Thus Concept 1.1.5 changes to

\[ e_k(\tau;F)=g_k(\tau;F), \quad k \in T(\tau). \]

For \(F=J^{\text{total}}(t-h',t)\), this direct term is \(d_k(\tau)-y_k(\tau)\) when \(t-h'+1\le\tau\le t\), and zero outside that loss interval. The loss still uses the model's output; only the value fed back into the recurrence is replaced by the target.

In RTRL, we treat the value of \(p_{i j}^{l}(t)\) as zero for any \(l \in T(t)\) when computing \(p_{i j}^{k}(t +1)\) via Definition 1.1.10.

\[ \begin{equation*} p_{i j}^{k}(t+1)=f_{k}^{\prime}\left(s_{k}(t+1)\right)\left[\sum_{l \in U \backslash T(t)} w_{k l} p_{i j}^{l}(t)+\delta_{i k} x_{j}(t)\right] \end{equation*} \]

Concept 1.1.12 : Pros and Cons of Teacher Forcing

Pros

  • Speeds up and stabilizes training (less compounding of self-generated errors).
  • Keeps trajectories on-target in continual/oscillatory tasks (helps learn correct phase/dynamics).
  • Efficient in continually operating nets, since teacher forcing injects truth states to keep trajectories on track, so gradients carry the right information.

Cons

  • Train/test mismatch: model is fed ground truth during training but not at inference → weaker free-running behavior (“exposure bias”).
  • Can mask error-recovery skills (model learns less about fixing its own mistakes).
  • Cuts some gradient paths (through forced units), which can under-train long temporal dependencies if overused.

docs.title: 1. PTB Dataset Prediction with RNN
docs.text:
Link to Code

Definition 1.1.13 : PyTorch RNN

PyTorch RNN Reference

\[ h_t = \tanh (x_t W_{ih}^T + b_{ih} + h_{t-1} W_{hh}^T + b_{hh}) \]

Here \(h_{t-1}\) is the previous time step's hidden state in the same recurrent layer. In a stacked RNN, higher layers receive the preceding layer's output at the current time as their input. The shapes below assume batched input, batch_first=False, and bidirectional=False.

Parameters :

  • input_size : \(H_{in}\), the dimension of input \(x_t\).
  • hidden_size : \(H_{out}\), the dimension of hidden state \(h_t\).
  • num_layers : \(K\), the number of recurrent layers, setting 2 layers means stacking two RNNs together to form a stacked RNN, with the second RNN taking the outputs of the first RNN and computing the final results.

Other parameters (given when inputs are given) :

  • sequence_length : \(L\), the sequence length of input \(x_t\).
  • batch_size : \(N\), the batch size of input.

Inputs :

  • input : \(x_t\), tensor of shape \((L, N, H_{in})\) containing the features of the input sequence.
  • hx : \(h_0\), tensor of shape \((K, N, H_{out})\), containing the initial hidden state. It defaults to zeros if omitted.

Outputs :

  • output : \(h_t\), tensor of shape \((L, N, H_{out})\) containing the output features from the last layer of the RNN, for each \(t\).
  • h_n : \(h_L\), tensor of shape \((K, N, H_{out})\) containing the final hidden state for each element in the batch.

Variables :

  • weight_ih_l[k] : input-hidden weights of the \(k\)th layer, of shape \((H_{out}, H_{in})\) for \(k=0\), \((H_{out}, H_{out})\) for \(k>0\).
  • weight_hh_l[k] : hidden-hidden weights of the \(k\)th layer, of shape \((H_{out}, H_{out})\).
  • bias_ih_l[k] : input-hidden bias of the \(k\)th layer, of shape \((H_{out})\).
  • bias_hh_l[k] : hidden-hidden bias of the \(k\)th layer, of shape \((H_{out})\).

In order to predict the next word in the PTB dataset with RNN, we constructed an embedding - rnn - linear structured model. First, we transformed each word into a feature vector using the embedding layer. After passing the sequence of feature vectors through the RNN, a linear layer produces vocabulary logits. Softmax converts these logits to next-word probabilities. For training, PyTorch's cross-entropy loss takes the logits directly and applies log-softmax internally.

# --- 4. RNN Model ---
class RNNModel(nn.Module):
    """Minimal RNN LM: Embedding → RNN → Linear-to-Vocab.

    Forward expects:
      tokens : [sequence_length, batch_size]
      h_0    : [num_layers,     batch_size, hidden_size] or None
    Returns:
      logits : [sequence_length, batch_size, vocab_size]
      h_N    : [num_layers,     batch_size, hidden_size]
    """
    def __init__(self, dict_size, embedding_size, hidden_size, num_layers):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(dict_size, embedding_size)
        self.rnn = nn.RNN(embedding_size, hidden_size, num_layers=num_layers)
        self.linear = nn.Linear(hidden_size, dict_size)

    def forward(self, x, h):
        """
        tokens   : [sequence_length, batch_size]
        h        : [num_layers, batch_size, hidden_size]
        embedded : [sequence_length, batch_size, embedding_size]
        out      : [sequence_length, batch_size, hidden_size]
        logits   : [sequence_length, batch_size, vocab_size]
        """
        emb = self.embedding(x)            # [seq_len, B, E]
        out, h = self.rnn(emb, h)          # out: [seq_len, B, H]
        logits = self.linear(out)          # [seq_len, B, V]
        return logits, h

Code 1.1.1.1 : Stateless Training on Truncated Windows using PyTorch RNN

Source file: 1.1.1.py.

# --- 3. Dataset Class ---
class PTBSequenceDataset:
    """Slice a long 1D corpus into (input, target) pairs of fixed sequence length."""
    def __init__(self, corpus, sequence_length):
        self.corpus = corpus
        self.seq_len = sequence_length

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.corpus) - self.seq_len

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        inputs = self.corpus[idx : idx + self.seq_len]
        targets = self.corpus[idx + 1 : idx + self.seq_len + 1]
        return inputs, targets

# --- 5. Setup ---
sequence_length = 35

train_set = PTBSequenceDataset(train_corpus[:100000], sequence_length)
test_set = PTBSequenceDataset(test_corpus, sequence_length)

train_loader = DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_set, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False)

This dataset creates overlapping windows of length \(L\), one for every valid starting position, and shuffles them for training. Each window starts with a zero hidden state, so the model has at most \(L\) input tokens of context within that window. This is stateless training on truncated windows, rather than stateful \(BPTT(L;L)\) on consecutive chunks of one stream.

The original run reported 5.31% test accuracy. However, the linked training and evaluation-loss code transpose inputs from \([B,L]\) to \([L,B]\) while leaving targets in \([B,L]\) order before flattening them. This pairs most logits with the wrong labels. Both tensors must use the same ordering:

# DataLoader returns inputs and targets with shape [B, L].
inputs = inputs.to(device).t().contiguous()
targets = targets.to(device).t().contiguous()
logits, _ = model(inputs, None)  # Zero initial hidden state.
loss = criterion(logits.reshape(-1, dict_size), targets.reshape(-1))

Apply the same target alignment when computing evaluation loss. The existing accuracy function already aligns predictions with targets by transposing predictions back to \([B,L]\); preserve that consistency if changing target layout. The low accuracy is therefore not evidence that stateless training cannot learn; a corrected run is needed for a fair comparison.

Figure 1.1.6 : Original stateless training curve, affected by the target-ordering bug.

Code 1.1.1.2 : Stateful TBPTT with PyTorch RNN

Source file: 1.1.2.py.

# --- 3) Stream batching into [T, B] ---
def batchify(data_1d, batch_size, device):
    """
    Reshape a 1D token stream into [T, B] where B=batch_size parallel streams.
    Trims the tail so T*B divides the length exactly.
    """
    n_batches = data_1d.size(0) // batch_size
    data_1d = data_1d.narrow(0, 0, n_batches * batch_size)
    data_tb = data_1d.view(batch_size, -1).t().contiguous()  # [T, B]
    return data_tb.to(device)

# --- 4) TBPTT windowing via IterableDataset (stateful order preserved) ---
class StreamBatchDataset(IterableDataset):
    """
    Iterates over a time-major source tensor [T, batch_size] and yields
    (data_window, target_window) pairs for TBPTT:
    data_window   : [seq_len, batch_size]
    target_window : [seq_len * batch_size]  (flattened next-token labels)
    NOTE: Order is sequential; do NOT shuffle if you want stateful training.
    """
    def __init__(self, source_tb: torch.Tensor, sequence_length: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.source = source_tb
        self.seq_len = sequence_length

    def __iter__(self):
        T = self.source.size(0)
        for i in range(0, T - 1, self.seq_len):
            cur_len = min(self.seq_len, (T - 1) - i)
            data = self.source[i : i + cur_len]                   # [cur_len, B]
            target = self.source[i + 1 : i + 1 + cur_len]         # [cur_len, B]
            yield data, target.reshape(-1)                         # [cur_len*B]

# --- 6) Hyperparameters & tensors ---
sequence_length = 35
# Create iterable datasets that yield TBPTT windows sequentially
train_ds = StreamBatchDataset(train_tb, sequence_length)
test_ds  = StreamBatchDataset(test_tb,  sequence_length)

# DataLoaders: keep order, no auto-batching (each dataset item is already a batch window)
# num_workers=0 is safest when source tensors live on GPU
train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=None, shuffle=False, num_workers=0)
test_loader  = DataLoader(test_ds,  batch_size=None, shuffle=False, num_workers=0)

For stateful training, we used iterable datasets. First, split the corpus into \(N\) parallel contiguous streams. Then, take consecutive windows of length \(L\) from each stream, carrying each stream's hidden state to its next window.

For stateful TBPTT, retain hidden-state values across windows but detach their computation graph before the next window (hidden = hidden.detach()). Reset the state when starting an independent sequence or a new pass through the corpus. Forward context can therefore extend beyond \(L\) steps even though gradients stop at each window boundary.

This run reported 23.66% final test accuracy. It also uses a different training-data setup from the 100,000-token subset in Code 1.1.1.1, so these runs do not isolate the effect of carrying hidden state.

Figure 1.1.7 : Stateful TBPTT training curve with improved accuracy.

Code 1.1.1.3 : Handmade RNN

Source file: 1.1.3.py.

Replaced the PyTorch RNN with custom implementations of class MinimalRNNCell(nn.Module) and class MinimalRNN(nn.Module).

Showed almost the same results as Code 1.1.1.2

docs.title: 2. Solving Delayed XOR Task with Various RNN Algorithms
docs.text:
Link to Code

The paper labels the output produced from input \(x^{\mathrm{in}}(t)\) as \(y(t+1)\), while PyTorch labels the output produced from \(x_t\) as \(h_t\). For a single recurrent layer, these are equivalent recurrences after relabeling time; this is not an extra computational delay in one implementation. The following convention makes the input/output and target alignment explicit.

Definition 1.1.14 : Universal Forward Pass Convention

Paper (Definition 1.1.1, Definition 1.1.2)

  • Forward pass : \(x(t) = [x^{\text{in}}(t), y(t)], s(t+1)=Wx(t), y(t+1)=f(s(t+1))\)
  • Supervision (targets) : At time step \(t\), we supervise the output \(y(t+1)\), produced after consuming \(x(t)\), with target \(d(t+1)\).

PyTorch (Definition 1.1.13)

  • Forward pass : \(h_t= \text{RNN}(x_t, h_{t-1})\)
  • Supervision (targets) : At timestep \(t\), we supervise \(h_t\), which was produced after consuming \(x_t\).
  • Alignment to the paper : Identify \(h_t \equiv y(t+1), x_t \equiv x^{\text{in}}(t)\)

Universal Convention

  • Forward pass : x_list[t] \(\equiv x(t)\), s_list[t] \(\equiv s(t+1)\), y_list[t]\(\equiv y(t+1)\) (\(x(t), s(t+1), y(t+1)\) is defined as the paper)
  • Supervision (targets) : D[t] \(\equiv d(t+1)\), At timestep \(t\), we compare y_list[t] to D[t], i.e. \(y(t+1)\) to \(d(t+1)\).
Concept Paper PyTorch Universal Convention External input used \(x^{\text{in}}(t)\) input[t]\(=x_t\) x_list[t][:m] Concatenated input \(x(t)\) — (implicit) x_list[t] = [x_in(t), y(t)] Pre-activation \(s(t+1)\) — (inside cell) s_list[t] Output/hidden \(y(t+1)\) output[t]\(=h_t\) y_list[t] = x_list[t+1][m:] Previous state \(y(t)\) output[t-1]\(=h_{t-1}\) x_list[t][m:] Target at timestep \(t\) \(d(t+1)\) answer[t] D[t]

Using the universal forward pass convention (Definition 1.1.14), we implemented and compared various algorithms of gradient computation in RNNs. We tackled delayed XOR: D[t + tau] is the XOR of the two bits in X[t]. Under the universal convention, D[t + tau] supervises y_list[t + tau], which is the paper's \(y(t+\tau+1)\). Thus \(\tau\) is a delay in array indices; the paper's output-time label includes the extra \(+1\).

Code 1.1.2

  • alg_pytorch.py : Used a single layer PyTorch RNN module described in Definition 1.1.13, modified to match Definition 1.1.14.

  • alg_bptt.py : The linked implementation truncates each supervised output's backward path separately to \(h\) transitions and updates every \(h'\) steps. When \(h'>1\), this differs from Concept 1.1.5: earlier losses in an update can reach further back than the single shared boundary \(t-h\). Its plot label "tbptt" should be read with this implementation-specific convention.

    • ebptt \(\equiv BPTT(\infty, \infty)\) : Epochwise BPTT defined in Definition 1.1.7.
    • rtbptt \(\equiv BPTT(\infty, 1)\) : Real-Time BPTT defined in Definition 1.1.6.
    • tbptt : per-loss truncation to \(h\) transitions, with an update every \(h'\) steps.

  • alg_rtrl.py : Implemented RTRL described in Definition 1.1.10. For analogy with BPTT, introduced \(RTRL(h')\), where we update the weights every \(h'\) timesteps.

    • ertrl \(\equiv RTRL(\infty)\) : Epochwise RTRL, accumulate gradients and update weights after consuming an epoch.
    • rtrl \(\equiv RTRL(1)\) : update weights every time step.

  • alg_hybrid.py : The linked prototype computes bucket-local BPTT gradients and maintains boundary sensitivities. However, its weight update does not use those sensitivities to add the gradient contribution through the bucket's initial state. The plotted "hybrid" result therefore represents this incomplete prototype, not the paper's exact \(FP/BPTT(h)\) algorithm.

  • core.py : File for dataclass definitions.
  • helper.py : File containing activation functions, their derivatives, delayed xor testbench, and scorers.
  • main.py : Main runner file, controls parameters, creates testdata, and runs the test on all algorithms.

One example configuration is shown below. The figures use different values of \(\tau\); Figures 1.1.9 and 1.1.10 also run for 10,000 epochs rather than the 7,500 shown here.

results = run_many(
    alg_names=["ebptt", "ertrl", "rtbptt", "tbptt", "rtrl", "pytorch", "hybrid"],
    m=2, n=8, lr=5e-3,
    tau=7, Ttrain=50, Teval=50,
    eval_seqs=200, quick_eval_seqs=50,
    epochs=7500, log_every=250,
    weight_decay=0.0,
    truncation_h=15, update_every_hprime=5,   # used only by tbptt
    rtrl_hprime=1,                            # used only by rtrl (continual)
    h_bucket=10,                              # used only by hybrid
    grad_clip=None,
    seed=0,
    metric_name="acc", metric_threshold=0.5,
)

Figure 1.1.8 : Delayed XOR accuracy at tau=5.

Figure 1.1.9 : Delayed XOR accuracy at tau=7.

Figure 1.1.10 : Delayed XOR accuracy at tau=10.

In these runs, all plotted implementations approached 100% quick-evaluation accuracy at \(\tau=5\), while learning generally became harder at larger delays. At \(\tau=10\), most curves stayed near the 50% chance level, although real-time BPTT rose above 60% near the end.

These observations concern this small RNN, its hyperparameters, and these implementations, including the prototype limitations above. They do not establish a fixed memory limit for all RNNs or a controlled ranking of exact gradient algorithms. LSTMs and GRUs introduce gating mechanisms that can make learning longer dependencies easier, but do not guarantee success on every long-delay task.

docs.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
docs.text:
Attention compares query vectors with key vectors and returns weighted sums of the corresponding value vectors. In self-attention, queries, keys, and values come from the same sequence; in cross-attention, queries come from one sequence and keys/values from another.

Definition 1.5.1 : Scaled Dot-Product Attention

  • Input Queries from \(S_1\) : From the first sequence \(S_1\), query vectors for each word are given as input.

    \[ q_1, q_2, \dots, q_{|S_1|} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}. \]

  • Input Key-Value pairs from \(S_2\) : From the second sequence \(S_2\), key-value vector pairs for each word are given as input.

    \[ k_1, k_2, \dots, k_{|S_2|} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}. \] \[ v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{|S_2|} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v}. \]

  • Score (relation) of word \(S_{1, i}\) and \(S_{2, j}\) : For each \(1 \le i \le |S_1|\), \(1 \le j \le |S_2|\), we compute the dot-product attention as the dot product between the query vector \(q_i\) and key vector \(k_j\). This value represents the score (relation) of word \(S_{1, i}\) and \(S_{2, j}\).

    \[ s(i, j) = q_i \cdot k_j. \]

  • Masking (Optional) : If we want to ignore the relation between specific pair of words, we can apply masking by zeroing out the softmax probability with explicitly setting

    \[ s(i, j) = -\infty. \]

    Causal masking is used in Definition 1.5.9; padding masks also exclude padding positions. Each valid query must retain at least one unmasked key for softmax to be well-defined.

  • Output : For each fixed \(i\), define the score vector over all positions in \(S_2\):

    \[ s_i = \big(s(i,1), s(i,2), \dots, s(i,|S_2|)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_2|}. \]

    We scale by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) and take softmax to get attention weights:

    \[ \alpha_{i,j} = \frac{\exp\!\left(\frac{s(i,j)}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)} {\sum_{t=1}^{|S_2|}\exp\!\left(\frac{s(i,t)}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)} \qquad (1 \le j \le |S_2|). \]

    Then the output (context) vector for token \(S_{1,i}\) is the weighted average of the values:

    \[ o_i = \sum_{j=1}^{|S_2|} \alpha_{i,j}\, v_j \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v}. \]

    Collecting all outputs gives:

    \[ o_1, o_2, \dots, o_{|S_1|} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v}. \]

  • Matrix form : Define the stacked matrices by putting the vectors as rows:

    \[ Q = \begin{bmatrix} q_1^\top \\ q_2^\top \\ \vdots \\ q_{|S_1|}^\top \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_1|\times d_k}, \qquad K = \begin{bmatrix} k_1^\top \\ k_2^\top \\ \vdots \\ k_{|S_2|}^\top \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_2|\times d_k}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} v_1^\top \\ v_2^\top \\ \vdots \\ v_{|S_2|}^\top \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_2|\times d_v}. \] \[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V = \begin{bmatrix} o_1^\top \\ o_2^\top \\ \vdots \\ o_{|S_1|}^\top \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_1|\times d_v}. \]

Among the commonly used additive attention and dot-product (multiplicative) attention, the paper chose dot-product attention, with a scaling factor of \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\). The scaling factor was introduced to normalize the dot-product, which grows bigger for larger values of \(d_k\), which will push the softmax function into regions where the gradients vanish. (Modeling the components of \(q_i\) and \(k_j\) as i.i.d. random variables of mean \(0\) and variance \(1\) gives \(s(i, j) = q_i \cdot k_j\) variance of \(d_k\), so we have to normalize by the scaling factor of \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\).)

Figure 1.5.1 : Scaled dot-product attention.

docs.title: Multi-Head Attention
docs.text:
Instead of using just one attention, we project the query, key, value vectors to \(h\) multiple heads and perform attention function on each of them in parallel. The outputs of the heads are concatenated and projected to obtain the final representations.

Definition 1.5.2 : Multi-Head Attention

  • Input : Queries, keys, and values for each token are given as vectors of dimension \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\).

    \[ Q \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_1|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, \quad K \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_2|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, \quad V \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_2|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

  • For each head, \(Q, K, V\) are projected to dimensions \(d_k, d_k, d_v\) by learned linear projections \(W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V\). Then, the attention function is computed for each set of projected queries, keys, and values.

    \[ W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}} \times d_k}, \quad W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}} \times d_k}, \quad W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}} \times d_v}. \] \[ \mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V) \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_1| \times d_v}. \]

  • Output : For each token, the results \(\mathrm{head}_i\) are concatenated, and projected again to output a vector of dimension \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\) by learned projection \(W^O\). Equivalently, partition \(W^O\) into one block per head, project each head with its corresponding block, and sum those projected outputs.

    \[ W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \] \[ \mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \dots, \mathrm{head}_h) W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{|S_1| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

Figure 1.5.2 : Multi-head attention.

docs.title: Position-wise Feed-Forward Network
docs.text:
Attention mixes information across positions, while the feed-forward network applies a nonlinear transformation to each position's contextual representation. Its parameters are shared across positions within a layer, but differ between layers.

Definition 1.5.3 : Position-wise Feed-Forward Network

  • Input : Representations of the tokens are given as vectors of dimension \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\).

    \[ x \in \mathbb{R}^{|S|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

  • Output : Each vector passes through two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between. Note that each token is passed through the feed-forward network independently.

    \[ W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}} \times d_{ff}}, \quad b_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff}}, \quad W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, \quad b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \] \[ \mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

docs.title: Positional Encoding
docs.text:
Without positional information or position-dependent masks, self-attention is permutation-equivariant and does not distinguish token order. Positional encoding is added to the input embeddings at the beginning to give the model information about the order.

Definition 1.5.4 : Positional Encoding

\[ \mathrm{PE} \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}} \] \[ \omega_i = \frac{1}{10000^{2i / d_{\mathrm{model}}}}, \quad \mathrm{PE}_{pos, 2i} = \sin(pos \cdot \omega_i), \quad \mathrm{PE}_{pos, 2i+1} = \cos(pos \cdot \omega_i). \]

For even \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\), use \(i=0,\dots,d_{\mathrm{model}}/2-1\). Each sine/cosine pair has wavelength \(2\pi\,10000^{2i/d_{\mathrm{model}}}\), forming a geometric progression from \(2\pi\) to just below \(10000\cdot2\pi\).

Figure 1.5.3 : Visualization of sinusoid positional encoding.

Concept 1.5.5 : Intuitions behind Choice of Positional Encoding Function

  • The binary representation of positions gives us a discrete (0/1) version of a positional encoding function: each bit is a separate “channel” that flips at its own rate. The least-significant bit changes every step (period 2), the next bit changes every two steps (period 4), then every four steps (period 8), and so on.

    \[ \begin{align} 0: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} & & 8: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} \\ 1: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} & & 9: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} \\ 2: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} & & 10: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} \\ 3: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} & & 11: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} \\ 4: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} & & 12: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} \\ 5: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} & & 13: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} \\ 6: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} & & 14: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{0}} \\ 7: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{0}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} & & 15: \ \ \ \ \color{orange}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{green}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{blue}{\texttt{1}} \ \ \color{red}{\texttt{1}} \\ \end{align} \]

    Sinusoidal positional encoding is the continuous, float-friendly analogue of the same idea, smooth sine/cosine waves with wavelengths (periods) increasing exponentially.

  • The sinusoidal positional encoding has a good representation of relative positions, \(\mathrm{PE}_{pos+\phi}\) can be expressed as a linear transformation (rotation) of \(\mathrm{PE}_{pos}\), for fixed \(\phi\) regardless of choice of \(pos\).

    \[ M_{\phi,i} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\omega_i \cdot t) \\ \cos(\omega_i \cdot t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\omega_i \cdot (t + \phi)) \\ \cos(\omega_i \cdot (t + \phi)) \end{bmatrix}. \]

    Here the transformation depends on the frequency pair \(i\):

    \[ M_{\phi,i}= \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\omega_i\phi) & \sin(\omega_i\phi)\\ -\sin(\omega_i\phi) & \cos(\omega_i\phi) \end{bmatrix}. \]

docs.title: Model Structure
docs.text:
Figure 1.5.4 : Transformer model architecture.

Definition 1.5.6 : Residual Connection + Layer Normalization

Each sublayer in the original encoder and decoder uses a residual connection followed by layer normalization (post-norm).

\[ \mathrm{LayerNorm}(x+\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)). \] \[ x, \mathrm{Sublayer}(x), \mathrm{LayerNorm}(x+\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)) \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

LayerNorm is applied independently to each row, normalizing across the dimension \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\).

docs.title: Encoder
docs.text:
The encoder takes the source sentence \(S\) as input, and aims to transform the sentence into a sequence of vectors that captures the meaning of the sentence.

Definition 1.5.7 : Encoder Layer

Each encoder layer consists of two sub-layers. Both of them are covered with residual connection + layer normalization (Definition 1.5.6).

  • Self-Attention Sublayer : In the self-attention sublayer, keys, values, and queries all come from the preceding encoder layer (or the embedded inputs in the first layer). No causal mask is applied, so each position can attend to all source tokens. A padding mask excludes padding positions in padded batches.

  • Feed-Forward Net Sublayer : The result of attention is passed to feed-forward net sublayer.

Concept 1.5.8 : Encoder

  • Input : The source sentence \(S_1, S_2, \dots, S_{|S|}\) is given as input.

  • First, after the source sentence \(S\) is embedded into vectors of size \(\mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\), positional encoding is added:

    \[ X^{(0)} = \sqrt{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\,\mathrm{Embed}(S) + \mathrm{PE}(S) \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

    Here \(\mathrm{Embed}\) denotes the unscaled embedding lookup; the paper scales it by \(\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) before adding positional encodings. During training, dropout is applied to this sum. It then passes through \(N\) encoder layers with identical structure (Definition 1.5.7) and independent parameters:

    \[ X^{(\ell)} = \mathrm{EncLayer}^{(\ell)}\!\left(X^{(\ell-1)}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}} \qquad (\ell = 1,2,\dots,N). \]

  • Output : The encoder outputs the final sequence of hidden states

    \[ Z = X^{(N)} = \bigl(z_1, z_2, \dots, z_{|S|}\bigr)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

    Each \(z_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) is a contextual representation of the source token \(S_i\) that incorporates information from all source positions via self-attention. In the decoder, \(Z\) is used as the key-value memory for encoder–decoder attention (cross-attention).

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
The decoder takes the target sentence \(T\) as input, and for each position \(i\) outputs the probability distribution of the next token that will appear after \(T_1, T_2, \dots, T_{i-1}\). In inference, the probability distribution is used to generate the next token. In training, we are particularly interested in the conditional probability that the next target token \(T_i\) will appear next.

\[ \Pr(T_i \mid S, T_1, T_2, \dots, T_{i-1}). \]

In order to assure that the output at position \(i\) only depends on the words with position less than \(i\), the decoder uses shifted inputs and causal masking in self-attention.

Definition 1.5.9 : Decoder Layer

Each decoder layer consists of three sub-layers. All of them are covered with residual connection + layer normalization (Definition 1.5.6).

  • Self-Attention Sublayer : In the self-attention sublayer, keys, values, and queries all come from the preceding decoder layer (or the embedded inputs in the first layer). Here, causal masking is applied so that words on the left cannot get information from the words on the right. (In terms of prediction, at the time when the left word is generated, the model does not know the words appearing right of it. Therefore, we block out the illegal "cheating" connections.)

    \[ \mathrm{MaskedAttn}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V, \quad M_{i,j}= \begin{cases} 0, & j \le i,\\ -\infty, & j> i. \end{cases} \]

  • Cross-Attention Sublayer : In the cross-attention sublayer, key-value pairs come from the final result of encoder, while the queries come from the result of self-attention sublayer. No causal mask is needed over the source sequence, but a source padding mask excludes padding positions.

  • Feed-Forward Net Sublayer : The result of attention is passed to feed-forward net sublayer.

Concept 1.5.10 : Decoder

  • Input : Let the target sequence include its end token, \(T_{|T|}=\langle\mathrm{EOS}\rangle\). Form the decoder input by shifting right by one position:

    \[ T^{\text{in}} = (\langle \mathrm{BOS}\rangle,\, T_1,\, T_2,\, \dots,\, T_{|T|-1}). \]

  • First, the decoder input is embedded and positional encoding is added:

    \[ Y^{(0)} = \sqrt{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\,\mathrm{Embed}(T^{\text{in}}) + \mathrm{PE}(T^{\text{in}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{|T|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

    Apply dropout to this sum during training, then pass through \(N\) decoder layers of identical structure (Definition 1.5.9), with independent parameters per layer:

    \[ Y^{(\ell)} = \mathrm{DecLayer}^{(\ell)}\!\left(Y^{(\ell-1)},\, Z\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{|T|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} \qquad (\ell = 1,2,\dots,N), \]

    where \(Z \in \mathbb{R}^{|S|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) is the encoder output (source “memory”).

  • Output logits and probabilities : The final decoder outputs are

    \[ Y^{(N)} = \bigl(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{|T|}\bigr)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{|T|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. \]

    For each position \(i\), let \(y_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) be the \(i\)-th row of \(Y^{(N)}\). A linear projection to the vocabulary size \(d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}\) produces logits, and softmax gives the distribution \(p_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}\).

    \[ P = \bigl(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{|T|}\bigr)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{|T|\times d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}. \]

    From the distribution \(p_i\), we take the probability of token \(T_i\) to compute \(\Pr(T_i \mid S, T_1, T_2, \dots, T_{i-1})\). Thus, we want to maximize the probabilities matching \(T^{\text{out}}\), where

    \[ T^{\text{out}} = (T_1,\, T_2,\, \dots,\, T_{|T|}), \qquad T_{|T|}=\langle\mathrm{EOS}\rangle. \]

Concept 1.5.11 : Shared Embeddings and Pre-Softmax Linear Transformation

For both the encoder and decoder, we use learned embeddings to convert the input tokens to vectors of dimension \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\). Therefore, the weight matrix of the embedding layer is of dimension \(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{source\_vocab}} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) and \(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\).

For the pre-softmax linear transformation in the decoder, we share the weight matrix with the embedding layer of the decoder. By transposing the embedding layer of decoder, we get the weight matrix of dimension \(\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}} \times d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}\), which we use to transform the decoder layer's output of size \(\mathbb{R}^{|T| \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) to \(\mathbb{R}^{|T| \times d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}\). This projection produces logits. Applying softmax across the vocabulary gives a conditional probability distribution at each target position.

The paper uses a joint dictionary for both the source and target language, thus sharing the same matrix for both of the embedding matrix and the pre-softmax linear transformation.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
Our goal in training is to maximize the conditional probability \(\Pr(T \mid S)\), given paired data \((S,T)\).

\[ \max_{\theta} \prod_{(S, T)} \Pr_{\theta}(T \mid S) = \max_{\theta} \prod_{(S, T)} \prod_{i=1}^{|T|} \Pr_{\theta}\!\left(T_i \mid S, T_1, T_2, \dots, T_{i-1}\right). \]

Equivalently, minimizing the negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy loss):

\[ \min_{\theta} \sum_{(S, T)} -\log \Pr_{\theta}(T \mid S) = \min_{\theta} \sum_{(S, T)} \sum_{i=1}^{|T|} -\log \Pr_{\theta}\!\left(T_i \mid S, T_1, T_2, \dots, T_{i-1}\right). \]

docs.title: Optimizer
docs.text:
Definition 1.5.12 : Adam with the Noam Learning-Rate Schedule

The paper uses Adam with \(\beta_1=0.9\), \(\beta_2=0.98\), and \(\epsilon=10^{-9}\). The learning-rate schedule, often called the Noam schedule, is defined below for optimizer step \(s\ge1\); the paper uses 4,000 warmup steps.

\[ \mathrm{lrate}(s) = d_{\mathrm{model}}^{-1/2} \cdot \min\!\left( s^{-1/2}, \; s \cdot \mathrm{warmup}^{-3/2} \right). \]

This corresponds to learning rate linearly increasing for the first \(\mathrm{warmup}\) steps, and decaying proportional to \(1/\sqrt{s}\) afterwards.

\[ \mathrm{lrate}(s) = \begin{cases} d_{\mathrm{model}}^{-1/2} \cdot s \cdot \mathrm{warmup}^{-3/2}, & s \le \mathrm{warmup}, \\ d_{\mathrm{model}}^{-1/2} \cdot s^{-1/2}, & s \ge \mathrm{warmup}. \end{cases} \]

Figure 1.5.5 : Noam learning-rate schedule.

docs.title: Regularization
docs.text:
Concept 1.5.13 : Residual Dropout and Label Smoothing

  • Residual Dropout : Apply dropout to the output of each sub-layer before it is added back through the residual connection and then normalized.

    Also apply dropout to the sum of token embeddings and positional encodings (in both encoder and decoder).

  • Label Smoothing : One common convention replaces the one-hot target distribution \(y \in \{0,1\}^{d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}\) with a softened target distribution \(y^{(\mathrm{ls})}\) over \(d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}\) classes:

    \[ y^{(\mathrm{ls})} = (1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ls}})\,y + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ls}}\cdot \frac{\mathbf{1}}{d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}. \]

    Then train with cross-entropy against \(y^{(\mathrm{ls})}\):

    \[ \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}} y^{(\mathrm{ls})}_k \log p_k. \]

    Other implementations distribute the smoothing mass only over incorrect, non-padding classes. The implementation below uses that convention and minimizes KL divergence to the smoothed targets. KL divergence differs from smoothed-target cross-entropy by the target entropy; neither is the hard-target negative log-likelihood used to define ordinary perplexity. The paper reports that label smoothing hurt perplexity but improved accuracy and BLEU in its experiments; such improvements are not guaranteed for every model.

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
In inference, we generate the output sentence token by token. Therefore, we start from token \(\langle \mathrm{BOS}\rangle\) and repeatedly run the decoder: at each step, we feed the tokens generated so far and predict the next token, until the special token \(\langle \mathrm{EOS}\rangle\) indicates the end of the sentence.

Concept 1.5.14 : Inference Workflow

  • Encoding (run once) : The source sentence \(S = (S_1, S_2, \dots, S_{|S|})\) is given as input and passed through the encoder (Concept 1.5.8) once. The encoder outputs

    \[ Z = (z_1, z_2, \dots, z_{|S|})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{|S|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, \]

    where each \(z_i\) is the contextual representation of the source token \(S_i\).

  • Auto-regressive decoding (repeat until \(\langle \mathrm{EOS}\rangle\)) : Initialize the decoder input as

    \[ T^{\text{in}}_{(1)} = (\hat{T}_0), \qquad \hat{T}_0=\langle\mathrm{BOS}\rangle. \]

    For step \(t = 1,2,\dots\), do:

    1. Run the decoder on the tokens generated so far and the encoder memory \(Z\):

      \[ P^{(t)} = \mathrm{Decoder}\!\left(T^{\text{in}}_{(t)}, Z\right) = \bigl(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{t}\bigr)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{t \times d_{\mathrm{target\_vocab}}}, \]

      where \(P^{(t)}\) contains probability distributions over the vocabulary for each position.

      With fixed weights, consistent positions, causal masking, and dropout disabled, earlier distributions are mathematically unchanged as the prefix grows (up to numerical differences).

    2. Predict the next token using the distribution at the last position \(p_t\):

      \[ p_t(w) = \Pr(w \mid S, \hat{T}_1, \hat{T}_2, \dots, \hat{T}_{t-1}), \] \[ \hat{T}_t = \operatorname*{argmax}_{w \in \mathcal{V}} p_{t}(w) \quad (\text{greedy decoding}). \]

      (Alternatively, use beam search or sampling.)

    3. Stopping criterion : If \(\hat{T}_t = \langle \mathrm{EOS}\rangle\), stop and output \((\hat{T}_1, \dots, \hat{T}_{t-1})\).

    4. Append and continue : Otherwise, append the predicted token to the decoder input:

      \[ T^{\text{in}}_{(t+1)} = (\hat{T}_0,\hat{T}_1,\hat{T}_2,\dots,\hat{T}_t), \qquad \hat{T}_0=\langle\mathrm{BOS}\rangle. \]

At step \(t\), naive implementations recompute \(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{t-1}\), which were already computed in the previous steps. In practice, modern Transformer decoders avoid this redundancy using a key–value cache (KV-cache). In each decoder layer's masked self-attention, keys and values for earlier positions remain unchanged under these inference conditions. Therefore, by caching the previous key-value pairs, we can optimize the algorithm by only computing the new distribution.

docs.title: Why Self-Attention?
docs.text:
Concept 1.5.15 : Why Self-Attention?

The paper motivates self-attention by comparing it to recurrent and convolutional layers for sequence-to-sequence modeling using three criteria:

  1. Computational complexity per layer : The paper compares \(O(n^2d)\) attention interactions with \(O(nd^2)\) recurrence, favoring the attention term when sequence length \(n\) is smaller than representation dimension \(d\). A full Transformer layer also includes \(O(nd^2)\) projections and feed-forward work; the comparison does not remove those costs. For very long sequences, the paper notes we can restrict self-attention to a local neighborhood of size \(r\) to reduce cost, at the expense of longer dependency paths.

  2. Parallelizability (sequential operations) : A self-attention layer connects all positions with an \(O(1)\) number of sequential operations, while a recurrent layer needs \(O(n)\) sequential steps (one per position). This makes self-attention far more parallelizable on modern hardware.

  3. Path length for long-range dependencies : Learning long-range dependencies becomes easier when the “path” between two positions is short. Self-attention yields the shortest maximum path length between any two positions (essentially constant), whereas recurrence and convolution require longer paths (recurrence grows with \(n\), convolution needs multiple layers to connect distant positions).

  4. Side benefit: interpretability : The authors also point out that attention weights can be inspected, and different heads often learn distinct, sometimes syntactic/semantic behaviors.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Link to Code

We implemented a Korean-to-English neural machine translator using the Transformer architecture. The run-specific figures below refer to the linked repository's logs/training_log_final.csv and saved evaluation outputs/evaluation_20251213_223618/.

Code 1.5.1

  1. Data

    • Sources : Moo, Tatoeba, AIHub datasets
    • Training : 1,698,151 pairs recorded in the final training log
    • Validation : 2,038 pairs recorded in that log
    • Evaluation : 4,390 saved source/prediction/reference triples
    • Preprocessing :
      • Empty-pair removal and token-length filtering (maximum 150 tokens)
      • Length ratio threshold: 3.5

    The earlier 897,566 / 1,896 / 4,061 counts describe an older preprocessing run and should not be combined with the final run's metrics.

  2. Tokenization

    • Method : SentencePiece (Unigram)
    • Vocabulary : 16,000 tokens per language (separate Korean/English)
    • Character Coverage : 0.9995
    • Special Tokens : <pad>, <unk>, <s>, </s> (built-in)

  3. Transformer Architecture

    Parameter Value d_model 512 d_ff 2048 num_heads 8 num_layers 6 (encoder) + 6 (decoder) dropout 0.3 max_seq_length 150 tokens total_parameters ~60M
    • Key Design Choices :
      • Separate vocabularies and embeddings for Korean and English
      • Weight tying between decoder embeddings and output projection
      • Positional encoding: sinusoidal (max 5000 positions)

  4. Training

    • Optimizer : Adam with the Noam learning-rate schedule
    • Learning Rate : factor = 2.0, warmup = 8,000 steps
    • Batch Size : 128 (effective: 256 with 2-step gradient accumulation)
    • Epochs : 50
    • Training Time : ~19 hours
    • Final Metrics :
      • Training KL loss against smoothed targets : 1.374
      • Validation KL loss against smoothed targets : 1.785

    The logger labels \(\exp(\mathrm{KL\ loss})\) as “perplexity” (3.95 and 5.96). These are not ordinary language-model perplexities, which require the mean negative log-probability of the true tokens.

  5. Inference

    • Method : Beam Search with KV Caching
    • Beam Size : 8 (4 groups for diversity)
    • Length Penalty : 0.6
    • Repetition Penalty : 1.5 (window: 30 tokens)
    • Diversity Penalty : 0.5

  6. Evaluation

    • Test Set: 4,390 samples
    Metric Score Corpus BLEU 18.04 Modified 1/2/3/4-gram precision (%) 51.31 / 24.13 / 13.96 / 8.45 chrF (character-only) 42.57

    These scores were recomputed from all 4,390 saved translations with SacreBLEU 2.5.1. BLEU signature: nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp|version:2.5.1. chrF signature: nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:yes|nc:6|nw:0|space:no|version:2.5.1.

    The original evaluator passed [[ref] for ref in references] instead of [references] to the corpus APIs. Reproducing that layout reproduces the old BLEU 38.02 and chrF 70.12, but it treats the references as separate reference streams of length one and scores only the first prediction. The precision components are individual modified n-gram precisions, not four cumulative BLEU scores. See the saved translations and SacreBLEU's Python API.

    • Error Analysis:
      • Repetition errors : 0.16%
      • Number mismatches : 13.49%
      • Unknown tokens : 0.00%
      • Length ratio : 1.00 ± 0.33

  7. Core Codes

The implementation combines regularization, training-stability measures, and efficiency optimizations. The training curves illustrate individual runs; they do not isolate the effect of each change.

Concept 1.5.16 : Dealing with Overfitting

The final configuration uses the following techniques. Dropout and label smoothing provide regularization; gradient clipping, accumulation, and mixed precision have distinct stability or efficiency roles.

  • Dropout (0.3) : Increased from 0.1 to 0.3 to regularize the model more strongly.

  • Label Smoothing (0.05) : Softened the one-hot target distribution to reduce overconfidence and improve generalization.

  • Gradient Clipping (max_norm = 1.0) : Limits gradient norms to reduce the effect of exploding gradients.

  • Early Stopping (patience = 10, min_delta = 0.001) : Configured to stop when validation loss no longer improves meaningfully; the final saved run completed all 50 epochs.

  • Gradient Accumulation (effective batch = 256) : Accumulates gradients over two microbatches before each optimizer update.

  • Mixed Precision (AMP) : Uses lower-precision operations where appropriate to improve throughput and reduce activation memory; the actual gains depend on hardware and workload.

The archived plots below retain their original labels. Their “Perplexity” panels show exponentiated KL loss, and their BLEU values use the incorrect reference layout described above; those values should not be read as valid corpus BLEU.

Figure 1.5.6 : Diagnostic run on 1,000 training examples, already using dropout 0.3 and label smoothing 0.05, showing a widening loss gap.

Figure 1.5.7 : Final 50-epoch run. Its data size differs from Figure 1.5.6, so this is not a controlled ablation of regularization. The BLEU and “Perplexity” panels retain the invalid metric labels noted above.

Concept 1.5.17 : Key Implementation Techniques

Here are the configured methods and their intended effects.

  • Hyperparameter tuning

    • Learning rate schedule :
      • Used the Noam scheduler with warmup = 8,000 steps (2× the paper default).
      • Set LR factor = 2.0 to reach a higher peak learning rate.
      • The original tuning notes targeted an earlier 897k-pair dataset; the final run used about 1.70M training pairs.
      • A longer warmup makes the early learning-rate increase more gradual; the logs do not isolate its effect on stability.
    • Dropout strategy :
      • Started with dropout = 0.1 (paper default) and increased it to 0.3.
      • Used higher dropout to compensate for the smaller dataset and reduce overfitting.
    • Batch size optimization :
      • Used physical batch size = 128.
      • Used gradient accumulation = 2 steps.
      • Achieved effective batch size = 256, balancing memory usage and training stability.

  • Repetition control (decoding-time)

    • Repetition penalty (1.5) :
      • Applied to tokens appearing within the last 30 positions.
      • Penalized recently used tokens to reduce repeated phrases.
      • The tuning notes projected a 40–60% reduction; no controlled before/after measurement is recorded with this evaluation.
    • Diverse beam search :
      • Used 8 beams divided into 4 groups.
      • Applied a diversity penalty = 0.5 between groups.
      • Encourages different beam groups to explore different token choices; this does not guarantee more natural translations.

  • Training optimizations

    • Mixed precision training (AMP) :
      • The implementation notes estimate 2–3× speedup and about 40% memory savings; those figures are not measured comparisons in the saved run.
      • The available evaluation does not establish that AMP leaves BLEU unchanged.
      • Implemented using PyTorch native autocast + GradScaler.
    • Gradient accumulation :
      • Processes microbatches sequentially while retaining accumulated parameter gradients, avoiding the activation memory of one larger batch.
      • Changes the number of samples per optimizer update; it is not itself evidence of improved convergence or reduced overfitting.

  • Inference optimization

    • KV caching :
      • Cached self-attention key/value projections during inference.
      • For output length \(N\) and fixed model dimensions, reduces total decoder self-attention work from \(O(N^3)\) when recomputing every full prefix to \(O(N^2)\) with incremental queries.
      • This comparison concerns the self-attention term; projections, feed-forward layers, cross-attention, and beam search also contribute work.
      • Used a design choice to cache only self-attention and recompute cross-attention (simpler, still fast).

  • Advanced decoding strategies

    • Beam search configuration :
      • Beam size : 8
      • Length penalty : 0.6
      • Repetition penalty : 1.5
      • Diverse beam groups : 4
    • Length normalization :
      • Used the form score / (length^α) with α = 0.6.
      • Counteracts the preference of summed log-probabilities for shorter hypotheses; the best penalty remains task-dependent.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Vector Spaces and Subspaces
docs.text:
Definition 2.1.1 : Complex vector space

The basic objects of linear algebra are vector spaces. The complex vector space of most interest to us is

\[ \mathbb{C}^{n}= \left\{\left(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\right)\mid z_{i}\in\mathbb{C}\right\} \]

The elements of a vector space are called vectors, and we will sometimes use the column matrix notation

\[ \left[\begin{array}{c} z_{1} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n} \end{array}\right] \]

in order to indicate a vector.

In \(\mathbb{C}^{n}\), vector addition is given by

\[ \left[\begin{array}{c} z_{1} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n} \end{array}\right]+ \left[\begin{array}{c} z_{1}^{\prime} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n}^{\prime} \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{c} z_{1}+z_{1}^{\prime} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n}+z_{n}^{\prime} \end{array}\right], \]

where the additions on the right are ordinary additions of complex numbers.

Scalar multiplication by a complex number \(z\in\mathbb{C}\) is given by

\[ z\left[\begin{array}{c} z_{1} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n} \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{c} z z_{1} \\ \vdots \\ z z_{n} \end{array}\right] \]

where \(z\) is a scalar, that is, a complex number, and the multiplications on the right are ordinary multiplications of complex numbers.

Physicists sometimes refer to complex numbers as c-numbers.

For convenience, we use the notation \(\left(z_{1}, \ldots, z_{n}\right)\) to denote a column matrix with entries \(z_{1}, \ldots, z_{n}\).

Concept 2.1.2: Quantum mechanical notation for a vector

The standard quantum mechanical notation for a vector in a vector space is the following.

\[ \begin{equation*} |\psi\rangle. \end{equation*} \]

Here, \(\psi\) is a label for the vector (any label is valid, although we prefer to use simple labels like \(\psi\) and \(\varphi\)). The \(|\cdot\rangle\) notation is used to indicate that the object is a vector.

The entire object \(|\psi\rangle\) is sometimes called a ket, although we won't use that terminology often.

Definition 2.1.3 : Zero vector

A vector space also contains a special zero vector, which we denote by \(0\). It satisfies the property that for any other vector \(|v\rangle\), \(|v\rangle+0=|v\rangle\).

Note that we do not use the ket notation for the zero vector - it is the only exception we shall make. The reason for making the exception is because it is conventional to use the 'obvious' notation for the zero vector, \(|0\rangle\), to mean something else entirely.

The scalar multiplication operation is such that \(z 0=0\) for any complex number \(z\).

Definition 2.1.4 : Vector subspace

A vector subspace of a vector space \(V\) is a subset \(W\) of \(V\) such that \(W\) is also a vector space. Equivalently, \(W\) is also closed under scalar multiplication and addition.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Bases and Linear Independence
docs.text:
Definition 2.1.5 : Spanning set, span, linear combination

A set of vectors \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |v_{n}\rangle\) is a spanning set for a vector space if every vector \(|v\rangle\) in that vector space can be written as a linear combination of vectors in that set.

\[ |v\rangle=\sum_{i} a_{i}|v_{i}\rangle. \]

In this case, we say the vectors \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |v_{n}\rangle\) span the vector space.

Example 2.1.6 : Two different spanning sets for \(\mathbb{C}^2\)

For example, a spanning set for the vector space \(\mathbb{C}^{2}\) is the set

\[ |v_{1}\rangle \equiv\left[\begin{array}{l} 1\\ 0 \end{array}\right] ; \quad|v_{2}\rangle \equiv\left[\begin{array}{l} 0\\ 1 \end{array}\right] \]

since any vector

\[ |v\rangle=\left[\begin{array}{l} a_{1}\\ a_{2} \end{array}\right] \]

in \(\mathbb{C}^{2}\) can be written as a linear combination \(|v\rangle=a_{1}|v_{1}\rangle+a_{2}|v_{2}\rangle\) of the vectors \(|v_{1}\rangle\) and \(|v_{2}\rangle\). We say that the vectors \(|v_{1}\rangle\) and \(|v_{2}\rangle\) span the vector space \(\mathbb{C}^{2}\).

Generally, a vector space may have many different spanning sets. A second spanning set for the vector space \(\mathbb{C}^{2}\) is the set

\[ |v_{1}\rangle \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\begin{array}{l} 1\\ 1 \end{array}\right] ; \quad|v_{2}\rangle \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\begin{array}{r} 1\\ -1 \end{array}\right] \]

since an arbitrary vector \(|v\rangle=\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\right)\) can be written as a linear combination of \(|v_{1}\rangle\) and \(|v_{2}\rangle\),

\[ |v\rangle=\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}}{\sqrt{2}}|v_{1}\rangle+\frac{a_{1}-a_{2}}{\sqrt{2}}|v_{2}\rangle . \]

Definition 2.1.7: Linearly dependent, linearly independent, basis, dimension, finite dimensional vector space

Let \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |v_{n}\rangle\) be a set of non-zero vectors. The vectors are linearly dependent if there exists a set of complex numbers \(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n} \in \mathbb{C}\), with \(a_{i} \neq 0\) for at least one value of \(i\), such that

\[ a_{1}|v_{1}\rangle+a_{2}|v_{2}\rangle+\cdots+a_{n}|v_{n}\rangle=0. \]

A set of vectors is linearly independent if it is not linearly dependent. Any two sets of linearly independent vectors which span a vector space \(V\) contain the same number of elements. We call such a set a basis for \(V\).

A basis set always exists. The number of elements in the basis is defined to be the dimension of \(V\).

In these notes, we will only be interested in finite dimensional vector spaces.

docs.title: 2.1.3. Linear Operators and Matrices
docs.text:
Definition 2.1.8 : Linear operator, identity operator, zero operator

A linear operator between vector spaces \(V\) and \(W\) is a function \(A: V \rightarrow W\) which is linear in its inputs.

\[ A\left(\sum_{i} a_{i}|v_{i}\rangle\right)=\sum_{i} a_{i} A\left(|v_{i}\rangle\right) . \]

Usually we write \(A|v\rangle\) instead of \(A(|v\rangle)\).

When we say that a linear operator \(A\) is defined on a vector space \(V\), we mean that \(A\) is a linear operator from \(V\) to \(V\).

The identity operator, denoted \(I_{V}\), is defined by

\[ I_{V}|v\rangle \equiv|v\rangle \]

for all vectors \(|v\rangle\). Where no chance of confusion arises, we write \(I\) instead of \(I_{V}\).

The zero operator, denoted \(0\), maps all vectors to the zero vector, as

\[ 0|v\rangle \equiv 0. \]

It is clear from the definition that once the action of a linear operator \(A\) on a basis is specified, the action of \(A\) is completely determined on all inputs.

Definition 2.1.9 : Composition of linear operators

Suppose \(V\), \(W\), and \(X\) are vector spaces, and \(A: V \rightarrow W\) and \(B: W \rightarrow X\) are linear operators.

Then we use the notation \(B A\) to denote the composition of \(B\) with \(A\), defined by

\[ (B A)(|v\rangle) \equiv B(A(|v\rangle)). \]

Once again, we write \(B A|v\rangle\) as an abbreviation for \((B A)(|v\rangle)\).

Concept 2.1.10 : Matrix representation

The most convenient way to understand linear operators is in terms of their matrix representations. The linear operator and matrix viewpoints are completely equivalent. The matrix viewpoint may be more familiar to you. To see the connection, it helps to first understand that an \(m\) by \(n\) complex matrix \(A\) with entries \(A_{i j}\) is in fact a linear operator sending vectors in the vector space \(\mathbb{C}^{n}\) to the vector space \(\mathbb{C}^{m}\), under matrix multiplication of the matrix \(A\) by a vector in \(\mathbb{C}^{n}\). More precisely, the claim that the matrix \(A\) is a linear operator just means that

\[ A\left(\sum_{i} a_{i}|v_{i}\rangle\right)=\sum_{i} a_{i} A|v_{i}\rangle \]

is true as an equation where the operation is matrix multiplication of \(A\) by column vectors. Clearly, this is true!

We've seen that matrices can be regarded as linear operators. Can linear operators be given a matrix representation? In fact they can, as we now explain. This equivalence between the two viewpoints justifies our interchanging terms from matrix theory and operator theory throughout the book. Suppose \(A: V \rightarrow W\) is a linear operator between vector spaces \(V\) and \(W\). Suppose \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots,|v_{m}\rangle\) is a basis for \(V\) and \(|w_{1}\rangle, \ldots,|w_{n}\rangle\) is a basis for \(W\). Then for each \(j\) in the range \(1, \ldots, m\), there exist complex numbers \(A_{1 j}\) through \(A_{n j}\) such that

\[ A|v_{j}\rangle=\sum_{i} A_{i j}|w_{i}\rangle \]

The matrix whose entries are the values \(A_{i j}\) is said to form a matrix representation of the operator \(A\). This matrix representation of \(A\) is completely equivalent to the operator \(A\), and we will use the matrix representation and abstract operator viewpoints interchangeably. Note that to make the connection between matrices and linear operators we must specify a set of input and output basis states for the input and output vector spaces of the linear operator.

docs.title: 2.1.4. The Pauli Matrices
docs.text:
Definition 2.1.11 : Pauli matrices \(I\), \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\)

Four extremely useful matrices are the Pauli matrices. These are \(2 \times 2\) matrices, written using several notations.

\[ \sigma_{0} \equiv I \equiv\left[\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \] \[ \sigma_{1} \equiv \sigma_{x} \equiv X \equiv\left[\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{array}\right] \] \[ \sigma_{2} \equiv \sigma_{y} \equiv Y \equiv\left[\begin{array}{rr} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{array}\right] \] \[ \sigma_{3} \equiv \sigma_{z} \equiv Z \equiv\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{array}\right] \]

Sometimes \(I\) is omitted from the list, with just \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) known as the Pauli matrices.

docs.title: 2.1.5. Inner Products
docs.text:
Definition 2.1.12 : Inner product, inner product space

An inner product on a vector space \(V\) is a function \((\cdot, \cdot): V \times V \to \mathbb{C}\) that takes two vectors \(|v\rangle\) and \(|w\rangle\) to a complex number. For convenience, we often write it as \((|v\rangle,|w\rangle)\). In standard quantum-mechanical notation, the same value is written as \(\langle v \mid w\rangle\).

The function \((\cdot, \cdot)\) is an inner product iff it satisfies the following:

  1. Linearity in the second argument:

    \[ (|v\rangle, \sum_i \lambda_i |w_i\rangle) = \sum_i \lambda_i (|v\rangle, |w_i\rangle). \]

  2. Conjugate symmetry:

    \[ (|v\rangle,|w\rangle) = (|w\rangle,|v\rangle)^*. \]

  3. Positive definiteness:

    \[ (|v\rangle,|v\rangle) \ge 0, \]

    with equality if and only if \(|v\rangle=0\).

A vector space equipped with an inner product is called an inner product space.

Definition 2.1.13 : Dual vector

The notation \(\langle v|\) is used for the dual vector to the vector \(|v\rangle\). The dual is a linear operator from the inner product space \(V\) to the complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\), defined by

\[ \langle v|(|w\rangle) \equiv\langle v \mid w\rangle \equiv(|v\rangle,|w\rangle). \]

The matrix representation of dual vectors is just a row vector. (It will be shown in Theorem 2.1.19.)

Theorem 2.1.14 : Conjugate-linearity in first argument

For vectors \(|w_i\rangle,|v\rangle\) and complex scalars \(\lambda_i\), any inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument, i.e.

\[ \left(\sum_i \lambda_i |w_i\rangle,|v\rangle\right)=\sum_i \lambda_i^*\left(|w_i\rangle,|v\rangle\right). \]

Proof

By conjugate symmetry,

\[ \left(\sum_i \lambda_i |w_i\rangle,|v\rangle\right)=\left(|v\rangle,\sum_i \lambda_i |w_i\rangle\right)^*. \]

By linearity in the second argument,

\[ \left(|v\rangle,\sum_i \lambda_i |w_i\rangle\right)=\sum_i \lambda_i\left(|v\rangle,|w_i\rangle\right). \]

Taking the complex conjugate yields

\[ \left(\sum_i \lambda_i |w_i\rangle,|v\rangle\right)=\sum_i \lambda_i^*\left(|w_i\rangle,|v\rangle\right). \]

Definition 2.1.15 : Inner product in \mathbb{C}^n

In \(\mathbb{C}^{n}\), the inner product between \((y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\) and \((z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\) is defined by

\[ \left((y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}),(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\right) \equiv \sum_{i} y_{i}^{*} z_{i} =\left[y_{1}^{*}\cdots y_{n}^{*}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c} z_{1} \\ \vdots \\ z_{n} \end{array}\right] \]

Concept 2.1.16 : Hilbert space

Discussions of quantum mechanics often refer to Hilbert space. In the finite dimensional complex vector spaces that come up in quantum computation and quantum information, a Hilbert space is exactly the same thing as an inner product space. From now on we use the two terms interchangeably, preferring the term Hilbert space.

In infinite dimensions Hilbert spaces satisfy additional technical restrictions above and beyond inner product spaces, which we will not need to worry about.

Definition 2.1.17 : Orthogonal, orthonormal, norm, normalized, orthonormal set

  • Orthogonal vectors: Vectors \(|w\rangle\) and \(|v\rangle\) are orthogonal if their inner product is zero. For example, \(|w\rangle \equiv (1,0)\) and \(|v\rangle \equiv (0,1)\) are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined by Definition 2.1.15.

  • Norm: The norm of a vector \(|v\rangle\) is

    \[ \begin{equation*} \||v\rangle \| \equiv \sqrt{\langle v \mid v\rangle} . \end{equation*} \]

  • Unit vector: A unit vector is a vector \(|v\rangle\) such that \(\||v\rangle \| = 1\). We also say that \(|v\rangle\) is normalized if \(\||v\rangle \| = 1\).

  • Normalizing a non-zero vector: For any non-zero vector \(|v\rangle\), the normalized form is

    \[ \frac{|v\rangle}{\||v\rangle \|} \]

  • Orthonormal set: A set \(|i\rangle\) of vectors indexed by \(i\) is orthonormal if each vector is a unit vector and distinct vectors in the set are orthogonal. Equivalently,

    \[ \langle i \mid j\rangle=\delta_{i j} \]

    where \(i\) and \(j\) are both chosen from the index set.

Theorem 2.1.18 : Gram-schmidt procedure

Suppose \(|w_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |w_{d}\rangle\) is a basis set for some vector space \(V\) with an inner product. There is a useful method, the Gram-Schmidt procedure, which can be used to produce an orthonormal basis set \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |v_{d}\rangle\) for the vector space \(V\). Define

\[ |v_{1}\rangle \equiv|w_{1}\rangle / \||w_{1}\rangle \| \]

and for \(1 \leq k \leq d-1\) define \(|v_{k+1}\rangle\) inductively by

\[ \begin{equation*} |v_{k+1}\rangle \equiv \frac{|w_{k+1}\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\langle v_{i} \mid w_{k+1}\rangle|v_{i}\rangle}{\||w_{k+1}\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\langle v_{i} \mid w_{k+1}\rangle|v_{i}\rangle \|} \end{equation*} \]

It is not difficult to verify that the vectors \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |v_{d}\rangle\) form an orthonormal set which is also a basis for \(V\). Thus, any finite dimensional vector space of dimension \(d\) has an orthonormal basis, \(|v_{1}\rangle, \ldots, |v_{d}\rangle\).

Proof

The vector in the numerator is orthogonal to each previously defined \(|v_i\rangle\) for \(1\le i\le k\) because each inner product with \(|v_j\rangle\) equals zero. Normalization makes \(|v_{k+1}\rangle\) unit length, and the construction proceeds inductively for \(k=1,\ldots,d-1\). The span is preserved by each subtraction step, so the resulting list of vectors spans \(V\).

From now on, when we speak of a matrix representation for a linear operator, we mean a matrix representation with respect to orthonormal input and output bases. We also use the convention that if the input and output spaces for a linear operator are the same, then the input and output bases are the same, unless noted otherwise.

Theorem 2.1.19 : Matrix representation of inner product and dual vector

Let \(|w\rangle=\sum_{i} w_{i}|i\rangle\) and \(|v\rangle=\sum_{j} v_{j}|j\rangle\) be representations of vectors \(|w\rangle\) and \(|v\rangle\) with respect to some orthonormal basis \(|i\rangle\). Since \(\langle i \mid j\rangle=\delta_{i j}\),

\[ \begin{align*} \langle v \mid w\rangle & =\left(\sum_{i} v_{i}|i\rangle, \sum_{j} w_{j}|j\rangle\right)=\sum_{i j} v_{i}^{*} w_{j} \delta_{i j}=\sum_{i} v_{i}^{*} w_{i} \\ & =\left[v_{1}^{*} \ldots v_{n}^{*}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c} w_{1} \\ \vdots \\ w_{n} \end{array}\right] \end{align*} \]

That is, the inner product of two vectors is equal to the vector inner product between two matrix representations of those vectors, provided the representations are written with respect to the same orthonormal basis. We also see that the dual vector from Definition 2.1.13, \(\langle v|\), has a nice interpretation as the row vector whose components are complex conjugates of the corresponding components of the column vector representation of \(|v\rangle\).

Definition 2.1.20 : Outer product

There is a useful way of representing linear operators which makes use of the inner product, known as the outer product representation.

Suppose \(|v\rangle\) is a vector in an inner product space \(V\), and \(|w\rangle\) is a vector in an inner product space \(W\). Define \(|w\rangle\langle v|\) to be the linear operator from \(V\) to \(W\) whose action is defined by

\[ (|w\rangle\langle v|)\left(|v^{\prime}\rangle\right) \equiv|w\rangle\langle v \mid v^{\prime}\rangle=\langle v \mid v^{\prime}\rangle|w\rangle \]

This notation is chosen so that \(|w\rangle\langle v \mid v^{\prime}\rangle\) may be read either as the result of the operator \(|w\rangle\langle v|\) acting on \(|v^{\prime}\rangle\), or as the result of multiplying \(|w\rangle\) by the complex number \(\langle v \mid v^{\prime}\rangle\), and these two meanings coincide.

Theorem 2.1.21 : Completeness relation

Let \(\{|i\rangle\}\) be an orthonormal basis for the vector space \(V\), and let an arbitrary vector be written as \(|v\rangle=\sum_i v_i|i\rangle\). Since \(\langle i \mid v\rangle = v_i\), we have

\[ \left(\sum_i |i\rangle\langle i|\right)|v\rangle = \sum_i |i\rangle\langle i \mid v\rangle = \sum_i v_i|i\rangle = |v\rangle. \]

Therefore for all vectors \(|v\rangle\), the operator \(\sum_i |i\rangle\langle i|\) returns \(|v\rangle\), so it equals the identity operator \(I\).

\[ \sum_i |i\rangle\langle i| = I. \]

This equation is known as the completeness relation.

Theorem 2.1.22 : Representing any operator in outer product notation

Suppose \(A:V \rightarrow W\) is a linear operator. Assume \(|v_{i}\rangle\) is an orthonormal basis for \(V\) and \(|w_{j}\rangle\) is an orthonormal basis for \(W\).

Using the completeness relation (Theorem 2.1.21) twice gives

\[ A = I_{W} A I_{V} \]

which expands as

\[ \begin{align*} &=\sum_{i j}|w_{j}\rangle\langle w_{j}| A|v_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i}|\\ &=\sum_{i j}\langle w_{j}| A|v_{i}\rangle|w_{j}\rangle\langle v_{i}|, \end{align*} \]

This is the representation of \(A\) in the outer product notation of Definition 2.1.20.

Thus \(A\) has matrix element \(\langle w_{j}| A|v_{i}\rangle\) in the \(i\)th column and \(j\)th row.

Theorem 2.1.23 : Cauchy-schwarz inequality

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is an important geometric fact about Hilbert spaces. It states that for any two vectors \(|v\rangle\) and \(|w\rangle\),
